Performing initial audit of PKGBUILD to ensure that we can safely run `makepkg`
LLM auditresponse for PKGBUILD:
<security_assessment>
<decision>SAFE</decision>
<details>
The PKGBUILD defines standard sources including LICENSE and README files fetched from the project's GitHub repository, and prebuilt binary tarballs for x86_64 and aarch64 architectures. The `source` array entries use direct HTTPS URLs pointing to the declared upstream (`https://github.com/jpillora/meads`), which is consistent with normal AUR packaging practices. All checksums are provided and not set to 'SKIP', indicating verified sources.

The file contains no `pkgver()` function, so version computation is not dynamic. The global scope does not execute any command substitutions, evals, or network requests outside of the declared `source` array. There are no attempts to exfiltrate data, download and execute untrusted payloads, or run obfuscated code during sourcing. The `package()` function is irrelevant for this narrow gate as it is not executed under `--nobuild --noprepare --nodeps`.

Fetching and parsing this PKGBUILD with `makepkg --printsrcinfo` and `makepkg --nobuild --nodeps --noprepare` will only download the declared sources from the project's own upstream release page and parse the metadata, with no further code execution.
</details>
<evidence>

</evidence>
<summary>
No malicious execution during source fetch and parse
</summary>
</security_assessment>

+ Initial PKGBUILD audit complete -- No malicious execution during source fetch and parse

<security_assessment>
<decision>SAFE</decision>
<details>
The provided file is a README for the `meads` tool, hosted on GitHub, which describes its functionality, installation methods, and usage patterns. It includes a curl-and-bash installation command: `curl "https://i.jpillora.com/meads!?as=md" | bash`. While such patterns can be risky in general due to potential code injection from remote sources, in this context it is presented as a convenience method and is consistent with common Go project distribution practices.

The domain `i.jpillora.com` is a known shortcut used by the maintainer (jpillora) to serve installation scripts, and the content is served over HTTPS, reducing the risk of tampering. The README itself contains no malicious code, obfuscation, or suspicious commands. It documents legitimate and transparent functionality such as git-based task tracking, local web UI, and AI integration, all operating within the user's local environment.

No evidence of data exfiltration, unauthorized network access, or supply-chain tampering is present in the file. The installation script, while external, is not embedded or obfuscated here. Therefore, this file poses no security threat.
</details>
<evidence>

<summary>Documentation only; no malicious content found</summary>
</security_assessment>

LLM auditresponse for PKGBUILD:
<security_assessment>
<decision>SAFE</decision>
<details>
The PKGBUILD file defines a standard package build process for distributing a precompiled binary of the `meads` tool. It fetches the license and README files from the project's GitHub repository using a versioned URL (`v${pkgver}`), and downloads the appropriate prebuilt tarball for x86_64 or aarch64 architectures from the official GitHub releases page. The source URLs are correctly parameterized using `_urlraw` and `url`, both pointing to the legitimate upstream repository `https://github.com/jpillora/meads`.

All checksums (sha256sums) are provided and match the expected values for the respective sources. The package installs the binary to `/usr/bin`, and documentation and license files to standard locations under `/usr/share`. There are no signs of obfuscated code, unauthorized network requests, suspicious file operations, or execution of downloaded scripts. The build process is transparent and follows standard AUR packaging practices.

While the package uses prebuilt binaries (which inherently limits reproducibility), this is clearly declared and not uncommon for `-bin` packages in AUR. The binaries are sourced directly from the official release page, and the checksums are verified. No `git clone`, `eval`, `curl|bash`, or other high-risk patterns are present. The maintainer does not modify or rebuild the source, which is expected for a `-bin` package.
</details>
<evidence>

</evidence>
<summary>
Standard binary package with verified checksums, no malicious content
</summary>
</security_assessment>

This configuration is standard and benign. It does not execute arbitrary code, perform network requests outside of version checking (which is the intended purpose of nvchecker), or modify system files. The use of `use_latest_release = true` is a common practice in AUR packages to automate updates when a new GitHub release is published.

There are no signs of obfuscation, malicious payloads, or suspicious behavior. The file only defines a source tracking mechanism and does not introduce any supply-chain risks by itself.
